title: SPA/619/2015 of Vijay Kumar Joshi AND OTHERS Vs Registrar Cooperative Societies Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
 Special Appeal No 619 of 2015
Vijay Kumar Joshi and others ..............Appellants
Versus
Registrar, Cooperative Societies and others ...........Respondents

Mr. Rakesh Thapaliyal, Advocate, present for the appellants.
Mr. B. D. Kandpal, learned Deputy Advocate General, present for the
State/respondent no.1.
Mr. Paresh Tripathi, Advocate, present for the respondents no. 2.
Mr. Manoj Tiwari, Senior Advocate, assisted by Mr. Alok Mahra,
Advocate for the respondent no.3.
Mr. C.K.Sharma, Advocate, present for the respondents no. 4 to 13.
.Coram : Hon'ble K.M.Joseph, C. J.
 Hon'ble U.C. Dhyani, J.
Dated: 24th October, 2016
K.M.Joseph, C. J. (oral)
 Appellants are respondents no. 3, 7, 9 & 15 in the writ
petition. The writ petition was filed by the 3rd respondent seeking
to declare inter se seniority positions of the appellants arbitrary and
illegal. The prayers in the writ petition were as follows:
" (i) Declare reversal of inter se seniority position of the
petitioner eight years after preparation of the earlier seniority
list, as arbitrary and illegal.
(ii) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
certiorari for quashing the impugned order dated 21.9.2013
passed by respondent no. 1 (Annexure no. 9 to the writ petition)

2
and seniority list dated 19.12.2011 issued by respondent no. 2
(Annexure no. 7 to the writ petition).
(iii) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
mandamus commanding the respondent no. 2 to place the
petitioner next to Shri Vinod Kumar Gupta in the seniority list
of Junior Branch Managers serving in the bank.
(iv) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
mandamus commanding the respondent no. 1 and 2 to promote
the petitioner to the post of Senior Branch Manager from the
date of promotion of her juniors with all consequential
benefits."
2. Briefly put, the case of the writ petitioner is as follows:
"The petitioner was appointed as Clerk-cum-Cashier in Nainital
District Cooperative Bank Limited, vide order dated 18.08.1987.
Thereafter, she was promoted as Junior Branch Manager in the
year 1994. A seniority list was prepared on 03.07.2002. Pursuant
to the directions, respondent no. 2 (Bank) re-determined the
seniority list dated 15.05.2003, in which the writ petitioner was
placed at serial no. 22. After Vinod Kumar Gupta. Respondents
no. 3 to 9 were placed below the writ petitioner. Respondents no.
10 to 14, who were working in Group III post of Clerk-cum-Cashier were promoted to Group II, as Junior Branch Manager on
21.09.2004, while respondent no. 16 was promoted as Junior
Branch Manager on 17.02.2010, but they are now being treated
as senior to the petitioner in the list issued on 19.12.2011.
Respondent no. 16 was not included in the seniority list dated
15.05.2003 as he was serving under a different employer on the
said date and came to be appointed in Nainital District
Cooperative Bank on 25.01.2007. The same is the case of
respondent no. 9 as he came to be absorbed in the Bank on
08.08.2003. Respondent no. 7 came through absorption on

3
28.08.2001 in the Bank from another Bank. One Dinesh Kumar
Tamta came through absorption on 03.08.1998. But, in the year
2011, all these persons were declared as senior and Dinesh
Kumar Tamta was promoted to Group 1 Post as Senior Branch
Manager on 16.12.2010 and respondent no. 7 was promoted to
the said post on 25.03.2013. Respondent no.3 (Vijay Kumar
Joshi), who is the first appellant before us, was appointed by
direct recruitment on 04.02.1995 and thus he is junior and was
rightly placed below the petitioner in the seniority list of
15.05.2003. But, in the seniority list of 19.12.2011, he was
declared as senior and on 25.03.2013, he was promoted as Senior
Branch Manager. Respondent no. 8 (Navin Chandra Bhatt) was
appointed on Group IV post, and on 04.05.1993, he was
promoted as Clerk-cum-Cashier and on 17.04.2003, he was
promoted as Junior Branch Manager. The seniority list prepared
on 15.05.2003, was treated as final and promotion was made on
the said post. It is stated in the order dated 25.03.2013 passed by
respondent no. 1 (Registrar), that five persons junior to the
petitioner were recommended for promotion to the post of Senior
Branch Manager. Petitioner's name has figured at Serial No. 22
in the said list. On 15.05.2003, Chandan Singh Negi, who is
placed at Serial No. 49 has been promoted. Petitioner, therefore,
filed a representation dated 06.01.2012 followed by two further
representations. Respondent no.2 (Bank) issued a seniority list on
15.11.2008, in which she was placed at serial no. 4 after Shri
Vinod Kumar Gupta. All the private respondents were placed
below the petitioner in the said list. However, in the seniority list
of 2011, this inter se seniority was disturbed. The earlier lists
issued in 2003 and 2008 were treated as final and on the basis of
these lists promotions were also made based on these lists. There
is no occasion to disturb the same. Persons up to Serial No. 3 in

4
the list of 15.11.2008 have already been promoted, therefore, it is
now the turn of the petitioner for promotion. But, in the seniority
list issued on 19.12.2011, petitioner is placed at serial no. 20 as
Junior Branch Manager serving in the Bank and the private
respondents have been treated as senior to the petitioner. Copy of
the seniority list dated 19.12.2011 is produced as Annexure-7."
3. The petitioner filed a representation dated 22.03.2013
followed by two reminders. The representation was rejected.
thereafter, on 21.09.2013. Thereafter, the petitioner approached
this Court on these facts.
4. Learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition. The
impugned order dated 21.09.2013 passed by respondent no.1
(Registrar) as also the impugned seniority list dated 19.12.2011
issued by respondent no.2 (Bank), was set aside. Respondent-authorities were directed to pass fresh orders in the light of the
impugned order.
5. It is necessary to notice paragraphs no. 11, 12, 13 and 14
of the judgment under challenge, which are as follows:
"11. As already referred above, the dispute before this
Court is regarding the inter se seniority between the
employees of District Cooperative Bank whereas the
petitioner was initially appointed as a Clerk-cum-Cashier
and thereafter in the year 1994, he was promoted to the
post of Junior Branch Manager. The respondents were
either promoted or were absorbed from another society to
Nainital District Cooperative Bank or some of them are at
least who are directly appointed as Junior Branch
Manager and others were already promoted to the post of
Senior Branch Manager. The determination of their
seniority has to be done under Regulation 26 of the
Regulations, 1975. As regarding the direct appointees, it
is absolutely clear in Regulation 26 (a) of the Regulations,
1975 that the inter se seniority of persons appointed by
promotion to any grade or category of posts shall be the
same as has been determined by the Board at the time of

5
selection. Meaning thereby the date if two or more
persons have been appointed by the Board their seniority
has to be done as per the list taken out by the Board.
Regarding the promotion the regulation 26 (b) of the
Regulations, 1975 clearly says that inter se seniority of
persons appointed by promotion to any grade or category
of posts shall be determined by their seniority in the post
held by them substantively prior to their promotion in
their feeding cadre which would mean that if 'A' is senior
to 'B' but for some reasons 'B' is promoted earlier then
'A' to the next higher post but whenever 'A' is promoted
to the next higher post "A" would regain his seniority and
would become senior to 'B'. This is called the "catching
up" principle. Regulation 26 (c) of the Regulations, 1975
determines the inter se seniority between promotees and
direct appointees.
12. It is an undisputed fact that the promotion to the post
of Junior Branch Manager is made from the feeding cadre
of Clerk-cum-Cashier. Therefore, it is made clear that any
of the respondents who are junior to the present petitioner
in the feeding cadre as Clerk-cum-Cashier though
promoted earlier then the petitioner to the post of Junior
Branch Manager on 08.01.1994 would become junior to
the petitioner as soon as petitioner is promoted. Similarly,
others who are senior to the petitioner in the feeding cadre
though promoted later than the petitioner to the post of
Junior Branch Manager will be deemed to be senior than
the petitioner in view of Regulation 26 of the Regulations,
1975.
13. Regarding the remaining employees such as the ones
who were absorbed or who are direct recruitees on the
post of Junior Branch Manager, the determination would
be that since they were not employees of Nainital District
Cooperative Bank Limited and were transferred here on
their own request they have been absorbed in the Nainital
District Cooperative Bank Limited with the condition that
they shall be put in the bottom of the cadre of Junior
Branch Manager which is again not in dispute and
therefore shall remain junior to the petitioner. Since their
date of absorption is subsequent to 08.01.1994 i.e. much
later than the petitioner was promoted to the post of
Junior Branch Manager.
14. It is further made clear that all direct recruitees who
have been promoted subject to Regulation 26 of the
Regulations, 1975, since regarding the petitioner to the
post of Junior Branch Manager is of 1993-94 and it will

6
close on 30.06.1994, any recruitment subsequent to that
date would also be shown to be junior to the petitioner."
6. The appellant nos.1 & 2 are shown as Senior Branch
Manager and appellant nos. 3 & 4 are working as Junior Branch
Manager.
7. Heard Mr. Rakesh Thapaliyal, learned counsel for
appellants, Mr. B. D. Kandpal, learned counsel for
State/respondent no.1, Mr. Paresh Tripathi, learned counsel for
respondent no.2 and Mr. Manoj Tiwari, learned senior counsel for
respondent no. 3.
8. Learned counsel for the appellants Mr. Rakesh Thapliyal
would submit that whereas appellant no.1 was directly recruited;
other appellants were absorbed subsequently from other
cooperative societies. In regard to the directions of the learned
Single Judge, the writ petitioner will be treated as senior to the
appellants and shall be put in the bottom of the seniority list. It is
contended by the learned counsel for the appellants that the
appellants, even assuming that they have given up seniority vis-a-vis petitioner, cannot lose seniority with respect to seniority of the
others, who was appointed much after the appellants in the cadre of
Junior Branch Manager. He would submit that the result of
accepting the judgment of the learned Single Judge is that though
the seniors of the writ petitioner have been appointed after the
appellants, they will get promotion from dates much anterior to the
actual dates of promotion. This is not contemplated in law. He has
contended that mere promotion on the basis of reservation will not
give consequential benefit of seniority. In this regard, he relied
upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of S.
Paneer Selvam and others vs. State of Tamil Nadu and others,
(2015) 10 Supreme Court Cases 292.

7
9. Learned counsel for the writ petitioner would submit
that appellants have accepted the bottom seniority and the effect of
the Rules according to learned Single Judge does not require any
interference.
10. In Union of India and Others vs. Virpal Singh
Chauhan and others, reported in 1995, 6 SCC 684, the Hon'ble
Apex Court was dealing with a case arising out of Railway
Service. The matter reached the Tribunal. The Tribunal had set out
the principles and the Hon'ble Apex Court, inter alia, held as
below:
"Under Article 16(4) there is no uniform or prescribed
method of providing reservation. The extent and nature
of reservation is a matter for the State to decide having
regard to the facts and requirements of each case. In
Indra Sawhney case it has been held by the majority
that "larger concept of reservations takes within its
sweep all supplemental and ancillary provisions as also
lesser types of special provisions like exemptions,
concessions and relaxations, consistent no doubt with
the requirement of maintenance of efficiency of
administration- the admonition of Article 335".
Therefore, it is open to the State, if it is so advised, to
say that while the rule of reservation shall be applied
and the roster followed in the matter of promotions to or
within a particular service, class or category, the
candidate promoted earlier by virtue of rule or
reservation/roster shall not be entitled to seniority over
his senior in the feeder category and that as and when a
general candidate who was senior to him in the feeder
category is promoted, such general candidate will regain
his seniority over the reserved candidate.
Notwithstanding that he is promoted subsequent to the
reserved candidate. There is no unconstitutionality
involved in this. It is permissible for the State to so
provide."
11. As far as the facts of this case are concerned, we would
think that this principle may not have any application. What is
stated, was that the candidate promoted earlier by virtue of rule of
reservation/roster over his senior in the feeder category will not be
entitled to seniority and that as and when general candidate, who
was senior to him in the feeder cadre is promoted subsequently,

8
such general candidate will regain seniority over the reserved
candidate. The Court found that the said principle is not
unconstitutional.
12. In this case as between the writ petitioner and the
appellants, the factual position is as follows in cadre of Junior
Branch Manager. The writ petitioner was promoted and appointed
as a reserved category candidate in a regular manner. Appellant no.
1 was directly recruited in the year 1995 i.e., after the writ
petitioner. Subsequently, appellant nos. 2 to 4, who had been
working in other cooperative societies, were absorbed in
respondent no. 2 Bank. All agreed that they will accept the bottom
seniority except one. Appellants no. 2 to 4 accepted the bottom
seniority. As far as the first appellant is concerned, he is appointed
after the date of regular promotion. The others, who were working
as senior to the writ petitioner in the feeder category on the post of
Junior Branch Manager, were promoted subsequently to the date of
promotion of the writ petitioner. On these facts, the learned Single
Judge, in our view, correctly understood the position that the
appellants' names will figure as juniors to the petitioner in the
cadre of Junior Branch Manager. Since persons, working as senior
to the writ petitioner in the feeder category for promotion as Junior
Branch Manager and they were subsequently promoted in the
cadre of Junior Branch Manager, i.e. subsequently to both the writ
petitioner and the appellants, and since they were senior to the writ
petitioner by virtue of Rule 26 (b) of the U. P. Co-operative
Societies Employee's Service Regulations, 1975 (hereinafter
referred to as 'the Regulation'), they have a right to have their
seniority fixed in the promoted category with reference to their
seniority in the feeder category. Now, a piquant position arises.
Seniors to the writ petitioner were all promoted after the
appellants. If we go by the principles of the date of appointment to

9
determine seniority in the cadre of Junior Branch Manager, the
appellants would figure as seniors to those seniors to the writ
petitioner. But, the facts of this case is that as the appellants will
figure as junior to the writ petitioner and the writ petitioner will
figure as junior to those, who were senior to petitioner and who
were promoted subsequently by virtue of the Regulation 26 (b).
Appellants would have to be placed below the writ petitioner and
consequently also below to those who were seniors to the writ
petitioner though promoted subsequently. As a consequence of the
Regulations in question, there is no other way to fix the seniority in
the facts.
13. Learned counsel for the appellants would contend that
since those were senior to the writ petitioner who was promoted
after the appellants have not been given promotion retrospective
date, the promotion would be treated as having only prospective
effect. Therefore, the seniority must be fixed with reference to the
date of promotion. In this regard, he refers to proviso to Rule 8 (1)
of the Government Servant Seniority Rules. We are not impressed
by the said arguments when there is no dispute before us. The
Regulation 26 (b) embodies the principle of catch up. It is not as if
the promotion will be treated as being made anterior to the date of
the promotion of appellants or of the writ petitioner. By virtue of
the principle of catch up notwithstanding the fact that the seniors
are promoted subsequently they will have the right to have the
inter se seniority to the higher category (promoted category) fixed
with reference to their seniority in the feeding category. Therefore,
it is not a question of granting notional promotion. It is the effect
of later promotion of the senior. In the context of regulations we
would not be in a position to accept the case of the appellants.
14. Learned counsel for the appellants also placed reliance
upon the judgment pronounced by the Hon'ble Apex Court in S.

10
Paneer Selvam and others vs. State of Tamil Nadu and others,
reported in (2015) 10 Supreme Court Case 292. Therein, the
Court was concerned with the issue relating to the effect of
insertion of Article 16(4-A). It inter alia reads as follows:
"17. The Constitution Bench held that Articles 16(4) and
(4A) did not confer any fundamental right to reservation and
that they are only enabling provisions. Overruling the
judgment in Jagdish Lal vs. State of Haryana, (1997) 6 SCC
538 case and observing that rights of the reserved classes
must be balanced against the interests of other segments of
society in para (77), this Court held as under:-
"77. We, therefore, hold that the roster-point promotees
(reserved category) cannot count their seniority in the
promoted category from the date of their continuous
officiation in the promoted post, - vis-à-vis the general
candidates who were senior to them in the lower
category and who were later promoted. On the other
hand, the senior general candidate at the lower level, if
he reaches the promotional level later but before the
further promotion of the reserved candidate - he will
have to be treated as senior, at the promotional level, to
the reserved candidate even if the reserved candidate
was earlier promoted to that level. We shall explain this
further under Point 3. We also hold that Virpal, (1995) 6
SCC 684 and Ajit Singh, (1996) 2 SCC 715 have been
correctly decided and that Jagdish Lal, (1997) 6 SCC
538 is not correctly decided. Points 1 and 2 are decided
accordingly."
18. Constitutional validity of Clauses (4A) and (4B) of Article
16 of the Constitution was challenged in M. Nagaraj And
Ors. vs. Union of India And Ors., (2006) 8 SCC 212. The
question that came up for consideration was whether by
virtue of impugned constitutional amendments, the power of
Parliament was so enlarged as to obliterate any or all of the
constitutional limitations and requirements upholding the
validity of the said Articles with certain riders. On the
concept of 'catch-up rule' and consequential seniority, this
Court held as under:-
"79. Reading the above judgments, we are of the view that
the concept of "catch-up" rule and "consequential
seniority" are judicially evolved concepts to control the
extent of reservation. The source of these concepts is in
service jurisprudence. These concepts cannot be elevated
to the status of an axiom like secularism, constitutional
sovereignty, etc. It cannot be said that by insertion of the
concept of "consequential seniority" the structure of
Article 16(1) stands destroyed or abrogated. It cannot be
said that "equality code" under Articles 14, 15 and 16 is
violated by deletion of the "catch-up" rule. These concepts
are based on practices. However, such practices cannot

11
be elevated to the status of a constitutional principle so
as to be beyond the
amending power of Parliament. Principles of service
jurisprudence are different from constitutional
limitations. Therefore, in our view neither the "catch-up"
rule nor the concept of "consequential seniority" is
implicit in clauses (1) and (4) of Article 16 as correctly
held in Virpal Singh Chauhan, (1995) 6 SCC 684."
19. In M. Nagaraj v. Union of India, (2006) 8 SCC 684 case
Court further considered two questions viz.:- (1) Whether
there is any upper-limit beyond which reservation is not
permissible? (2) Whether there is any limit to which seats
can be reserved in a particular year; in other words, the
issue is whether the percentage limit applies only on the
total number of posts in the cadre or to the percentage of
posts advertised every year as well? Answering the said
questions in paras (121) and (123), this Court held as
under:-
"121. The impugned constitutional amendments by which
Articles 16(4-A) and 16(4-B) have been inserted flow from
Article 16(4). They do not alter the structure of Article
16(4). They retain the controlling factors or the compelling
reasons, namely, backwardness and inadequacy of
representation which enables the States to provide for
reservation keeping in mind the overall efficiency of the
State administration under Article 335. These impugned
amendments are confined only to SCs and STs. They do
not obliterate any of the constitutional requirements,
namely, ceiling limit of 50% (quantitative limitation), the
concept of creamy layer (qualitative exclusion), the sub-classification between OBCs on one hand and SCs and
STs on the other hand as held in Indra Sawhney, 1992
Suppl. (3) SCC 217, the concept of post-based roster with
inbuilt concept of replacement as held in R.K. Sabharwal,
(1995) 2 SCC 745.
123. However, in this case, as stated above, the main issue
concerns the "extent of reservation". In this regard the State
concerned will have to show in each case the existence of the
compelling reasons, namely, backwardness, inadequacy of
representation and overall administrative efficiency before
making provision for reservation. As stated above, the
impugned provision is an enabling provision. The State is
not bound to make reservation for SCs/STs in matters of
promotions. However, if they wish to exercise their discretion
and make such provision, the State has to collect
quantifiable data showing backwardness of the class and
inadequacy of representation of that class in public
employment in addition to compliance with Article 335. It is
made clear that even if the State has compelling reasons, as
stated above, the State will have to see that its reservation
provision does not lead to excessiveness so as to breach the
ceiling limit of 50% or obliterate the creamy layer or extend
the reservation indefinitely."

12
The Constitution Bench judgment in Nagaraj case (supra)
was subsequently followed in Shiv Nath Prasad vs. Saran Pal
Jeet Singh Tulsi And Ors., (2008) 3 SCC 80 and Chairman
And Managing Director, Central Bank of India And Ors. vs.
Central Bank of India SC/ST Employees Welfare Association
And Ors., 2015 (1) SCALE 169.
20. While considering the validity of Section 3(7) of Uttar
Pradesh Public Services (Reservation for Scheduled Castes,
Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes) Act, 1994,
and Rule 8A of U.P. Government Servants Seniority Rules,
1991 which provided for consequential seniority in
promotions given to SCs/STs by virtue of rule of
reservation/roster and holding that Section 3(7) of the 1994
Act and Rule 8A of 1991 Rules are ultra vires as they run
counter to the dictum in M. Nagaraj's case in Uttar Pradesh
Power Corporation Limited vs. Rajesh Kumar And Ors., (2012)
7 SCC 1, in paragraph (81), this Court summarized the
principles as under:
"(i) Vesting of the power by an enabling provision may be
constitutionally valid and yet "exercise of power" by the
State in a given case may be arbitrary, particularly, if the
State fails to identify and measure the backwardness and
inadequacy keeping in mind the efficiency of service as
required under Article 335.
(ii) Article 16(4) which protects the interests of certain
sections of the society has to be balanced against Article
16(1) which protects the interests of every citizen of the
entire society. They should be harmonized because they
are restatements of the principle of equality under Article
14.
(iii) Each post gets marked for the particular category of
candidates to be appointed against it and any subsequent
vacancy has to be filled by that category candidate.
(iv) The appropriate Government has to apply the cadre
strength as a unit in the operation of the roster in order
to ascertain whether a given class/group is adequately
represented in the service. The cadre strength as a unit
also ensures that the upper ceiling limit of 50% is not
violated. Further, roster has to be post-specific and not
vacancy based.
(v) The State has to form its opinion on the quantifiable
data regarding adequacy of representation. Clause (4-A) of
Article 16 is an enabling provision. It gives freedom to the
State to provide for reservation in matters of promotion.
Clause (4-A) of Article 16 applies only to SCs and STs.
The said clause is carved out of Article 16(4-A). Therefore,
clause (4-A) will be governed by the two compelling
reasons-"backwardness" and "inadequacy of
representation", as mentioned in Article 16(4). If the said
two reasons do not exist, then the enabling provision
cannot be enforced.
(vi) If the ceiling limit on the carry over of unfilled
vacancies is removed, the other alternative time factor
comes in and in that event, the timescale has to be
imposed in the interest of efficiency in administration as

13
mandated by Article 335. If the timescale is not kept, then
posts will continue to remain vacant for years which
would be detrimental to the administration. Therefore, in
each case, the appropriate Government will now have to
introduce the duration depending upon the fact situation.
(vii) If the appropriate Government enacts a law providing
for reservation without keeping in mind the parameters in
Article 16(4) and Article 335, then this Court will certainly
set aside and strike down such legislation.
(viii) The constitutional limitation under Article 335 is
relaxed and not obliterated. As stated above, be it
reservation or evaluation, excessiveness in either would
result in violation of the constitutional mandate. This
exercise, however, will depend on the facts of each case.
(ix) The concepts of efficiency, backwardness and
inadequacy of representation are required to be identified
and measured. That exercise depends on the availability
of data. That exercise depends on numerous factors. It is
for this reason that the enabling provisions are required
to be made because each competing claim seeks to
achieve certain goals. How best one should optimize these
conflicting claims can only be done by the administration
in the context of local prevailing conditions in public
employment.
(x) Article 16(4), therefore, creates a field which enables a
State to provide for reservation provided there exists
backwardness of a class and inadequacy of
representation in employment. These are compelling
reasons. They do not exist in Article 16(1). It is only when
these reasons are satisfied that a State gets the power to
provide for reservation in the matter of employment."
21. In the light of the above, we shall consider the factual
matrix and the rival contentions urged and the purport of
Rule 12 of Tamil Nadu Highways Engineering Service Rules.
22. Dr. Rajiv Dhawan, learned Senior Counsel for the
appellants submitted that while it is well-settled law
followed by this Court in a catena of cases M. Nagaraj And
Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors., (2006) 8 SCC 212 that Article
16 (4A) is only an enabling provision and does not
automatically confer right on the reserved categories and
when no policy decision was taken by the State, Article 16
(4A) does not per se applicable to Tamil Nadu Highways
Engineering Service conferring consequential seniority to the
Junior Engineers who obtained accelerated promotion by
following rule of reservation. It was further submitted that
post of Assistant Engineers to be promoted as ADEs
constitute more than 75% of the cadre strength and by not
applying the 'catch up rule' among the Assistant Divisional
Engineers promoted from Junior Engineers by following rule
of reservation would result in patent discrimination creating
disharmony amongst the cadre. On behalf of the appellants,
it was urged that the implementation of the impugned
judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court would
result in conferring seniority to a less qualified and less
experienced Assistant Divisional Engineer appointed from

14
Junior Engineer belonging to SC/ST category and who
stand on a higher footing both on education and experience
than the Assistant Divisional Engineers belonging to general
category would offend the rule of equality.
23. Per contra, learned Senior Counsel Mr. R. Thiagarajan
and Ms. Kiran Suri appearing for the respondents
contended that there is no common list of seniority of the
appellants who are the direct recruit Assistant Engineers
and the respondents who are in the cadre of Junior
Engineers and, therefore, the services of the appellants and
the respondents cannot be compared and the 'catch up rule'
is not applicable. The learned Senior Counsel further
contended that promotion given to the respondents were not
accelerated promotion but promotion on account of rule of
reservation following Rule 12 of Tamil Nadu Highways
Engineering Service Rules. The respondents contended that
Article 16 (4A) of the Constitution has been added to protect
the consequential seniority arising out of accelerated
promotions and when such amendment is held to be valid
and not ultra vires the Constitution by this Court in M.
Nagaraj case (supra), the Single Judge ought not to have
allowed the writ petitions and the Division Bench rightly set
aside the order of the Single Judge.
24. Article 16(4A) of the Constitution is only an enabling
provision which specifically provides that the concerned
State may make any provision for providing reservation of
appointments or posts in favour of any backward class
citizens which is not adequately represented in the services
under the State. Articles 16(4) and 16(4A) have to be read
with Article 335 of the Constitution which deal with norms
of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to services and
posts and lay down that the claims of the members of the
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes shall be taken
into consideration consistently with the maintenance of
efficiency of administration, in the making of appointments
to services and posts in connection with the affairs of the
Union or of a State. In the absence of any policy decision
taken by the State of Tamil Nadu, Eighty-fifth Amendment
per se will not protect the consequential seniority granted to
the respondents who were promoted to the post of Assistant
Divisional Engineers following the rule of reservation."
15. In fact, in the said case, the Court directed that seniority
must be determined with reference to the catch up rule and there is
no scope for according seniority to a candidate belonging to the
reserved category, who got accelerated promotion vis-à-vis those
who are his seniors in the feeder category who came to be
promoted subsequently. Therefore, this is against the contention of
the appellants. In this case also, in terms of Regulation 26 placed

15
the petitioner, who was a member of the reserved category will not

16. Again, in fact, Mr. Rakesh Thapaliyal, learned counsel
for the appellants laid emphasis on para 17 of the judgment of the
Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Ajeet Singh and others (II) vs.
State of Punjab and others, reported in (1999) 7 Supreme Court
Case 209, which reads as follows:
"17. We shall at the outset deal with the contention raised
by Shri D.D.Thakur, learned Senior Counsel appearing for
the reserved candidates that Article 16(4) must be
interpreted keeping in mind the conditions prevailing fifty
years ago when the Constitution was drafted and when
Article 16(4) was incorporated in the Constitution. Learned
counsel submitted that the founding fathers were
conscious that a special provision for reservation was
necessary to see that the backward classes of citizens were
adequately represented in the services. Hence an
interpretation which would advance the said objective must
be applied. Reliance was also placed on the Statement of
Objects and Reasons in connection with the incorporation
of Article 16(4-A). In fact, all the learned counsel appearing
for the reserved candidates contended that the said officers
could not be treated as equals to the general candidates
and that their backwardness and past social oppression
must be borne in mind."
17. We would think again that this does not advance the
case of the appellants. What is stated in that paragraph, which we
have also extracted, is that the person belonging to the reserved
category cannot claim seniority by virtue of earlier promotion. But,
it is relevant to ask as against whom he cannot claim the seniority.
It is as against the candidate belonging to the general candidate
who are the seniors and who are promoted subsequently. In fact in
this case also, learned Single Judge held that the persons senior to

18. Learned counsel for the appellants would submit that the
promotions have not been challenged. Promotions, accorded to the
first appellant and the second appellant, have not been challenged.
According to the learned Senior Counsel for the writ petitioner, the
seniority list is being set aside. Since the promotions of the
appellants are not challenged, we make it clear that we have not
pronounced anything on the validity of these promotions.
19. Subject to the same the appeal is dismissed.
